To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

Our own teacher put it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. That was a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. The poet confesses the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. Asked about the Trinity, we answer from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Then we guard the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected.

And we read him everywhere in symbol - the raza and the shrara, the sign and the truth it carries. Eden points toward his cross, Adam toward him, the ark toward his church. Scripture's words were not problems to be solved but mysteries to be sung.

What we had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story. The Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete - the Gospel of the Mixed - the harmony our churches read in worship, not four separate books. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events.

Our own cherished story says an apostle came to our king, and the king wrote to Jesus himself. We will tell you that story honestly for what it is: our own legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When the sources begin - a church building destroyed in the great flood, the year 201 - the practices were already there. The one Gospel already the standard. Assembly on the first day, fasting, the covenant already established enough to need correcting. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. We said that out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

And we knew God as the one who stands with the persecuted. On the Persian side of our world, under a hostile crown, we learned to ask where he was when the blow landed. Our teacher answered with a roll-call: Abel, murdered. Jacob, persecuted and fled. Joseph, sold into the pit. Moses, fled to Midian. David at Saul's hand. And Jesus. The persecuted stand in the longest line Scripture keeps, and God's answer was never exemption - it was presence, and resurrection after.

Our honest answer: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order. 

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. Our sharpest doctrinal work happened in hymns and letters, not in decrees. One teacher would answer another by name - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - in verse meant to be sung, carrying the argument into the body so the congregation learned what we held by keeping the tune. The evidence for how it worked is exactly that: letters that name their recipients and date themselves to the year, and hymns copied into books that still exist. What we cannot show you is a hierarchy that could have enforced any of it.

Yes. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith - and faith, our teacher taught, is a building. It rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer but the prying scrutinizer - the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. The sage records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight.

For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Our own teacher said it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. What we knew, and what we kept, was faith that is contested, questioned, and still growing.

That was our picture: not a guilty infant, but a wounded humanity healed by the Physician.

A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. The last decades before the synod are nearly blank. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

What would survive scrutiny is the core itself: how we read Scripture as raza and shrara - symbol bound to the truth it carries. That the one woven Gospel was ours to sing and hear. That the covenant stood at our center early enough to need correction, not founding. And that our argument with the Jews survives entirely one-sided. What would not survive is any claim we settled who finally spoke for us. That question stayed open while we lived.

You are reading for information, and we read for mystery. That is the difference, stated plainly.

A word in Scripture - Eden, the ark, a pearl - was to us a raza, a sign bound to the truth it carries. The truth is the shrara. The two cannot be torn apart. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the Jordan toward the font. Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it - the whole creation, the Kingdom, the way light lives inside a small round stone. A single thing held that much, because God made it to hold it.

You are looking for what happened, or what a verse plainly says. We were looking for what it carries beneath its surface - the hidden truth woven into the sign from the beginning. That is not us making things up. It is us holding that God put the truth there to be found.

A madrasha - our teaching-hymn - could take one verse and unfold it for a congregation until the whole room saw what it carried. That was how we met the text: not to get through it, but to live inside it until it showed us what it held.

What you are missing is not information. It is the way we read.

Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women - the qyama - carried a standing of their own. They were bound to celibacy and service for life, and they stayed in town among their own people rather than leaving for the desert. By the time our record opens plainly on them, they were already established enough to need correcting, not founding. Their choirs carried our hymns into every congregation. The daughters sang alongside the sons. That was visible, public, and real.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name. Teaching authority did not always arrive through office.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. Whether the covenant order itself had a formal internal structure - a rule, an enclosure, ranks within it - our own record does not settle. We will not invent one to fill that silence.

We have no record that we saw our failures as failures - and that is the honest, uncomfortable answer. 

Our own hardest tools for restoration were real: confession, the medicine of penitence, and being brought back into the community afterward. The sage taught that healing comes from showing the wound to one who can help, not from hiding it. The physician is not allowed to shame the one who comes, or to tell others what was shown him. And the fallen fighter, once healed, goes back into the line. That machinery was there, and it was used.

But those were tools for the person who had fallen - not for the community examining its own conscience. Our sharpest voice flattened three different rivals into one word, deception, and truth was not always served by the flattening. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side of it - page after page, with no answering voice preserved. What we cannot show you is anyone among us troubled by that silence at the time. 

Our tools for the wounded believer were plain and pastoral: visit our Lord in the persons of the sick, the sage taught. In the famine year, as the next age remembered it, our poet arranged shelter and care for the dying, and told the people plainly to trust him with the means to do it. 

But for our own blind spots - where the community itself had been the wound - our tools were the same as every age's: too few.

The Syriac-speaking churches that carry our language and some of our hymns forward - the Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox, the Maronites - each traveled through centuries we did not see, and each was shaped by councils, splits, and settlements that came after our own years closed. The Diatessaron, the one woven Gospel we read in worship, was replaced centuries ago by the four separate books. The covenant as we knew it - men and women vowed for life but still living in town among their own kin - changed form over the generations that followed us. We are not their direct ancestor in an unbroken line. We are one stage they passed through, centuries before any of them became what they are now.

We cannot walk you through it step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. The sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order - our own record never wrote down.

What we can tell you honestly is this. A person was taught before they were baptized. Our own teacher wrote that it is right for the preachers of the church to warn someone clearly, before baptism, about everything the covenant asks. The Gospel they heard was one continuous story - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed, the four accounts woven together into a single telling. And they were taught to read it for what lay beneath its surface: the raza, the symbol bound to the truth it carries, so that Eden answered the cross and the Jordan answered the font. That was how we read Scripture - always looking for the truth the sign discloses.

At baptism itself they received the Holy Spirit, in what we called a second birth. They came up from the water sealed - marked with a sign we held as real. And some, not all, took the covenant vow at that same moment: the qyama, binding themselves for life to celibacy and service, staying in town among their own kin rather than leaving for the desert. The covenant stood at our community's core early enough that the first time a teacher wrote to them directly, he was correcting what they were already doing, not founding something new. Men and women both took it - the sons and daughters of the covenant, also called ihidaye, the Single Ones, a name that joined their own undivided lives to Christ the Only-Begotten.

That much we can show you. What we cannot show you is the exact sequence, spoken word by word. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we do not have.

We cannot give you one typical day, because what survives from us was written by the vowed celibates - the qyama, our covenant - not by the ordinary married householders who made up most of any congregation. So we will tell you honestly what we can show, and name plainly where the record thins to nothing.

For a son or daughter of the covenant, the day turned on prayer, fasting, and the service owed to the assembly. They rose early - the vigil was theirs to keep. They gathered with the rest of the congregation on the first day of the week, and the daughters among them sang the madrashe, the teaching hymns, so the whole church learned the faith by keeping the tune. A vowed man might serve as a deacon, or care for the sick; a vowed woman remained among her own kin, in her own town, not shut away. The fast they kept was stricter than what the rest carried, and the celibacy was for life. That standing - earned by the vow, not by office - carried real weight in the congregation.

What we cannot show you is an ordinary married believer's day in their own words. They were there - most of our people married, raised children, worked, and the congregations were full of them. But they left no diary, no letter describing their own morning or their own work. The enslaved, if there were any among us, left nothing at all. And the women whose voices carried our hymns to the whole church - the daughters of the covenant, whose singing everyone heard - had not one line of their own kept.

We will not invent a fuller picture to fill that silence. What we can offer you is one morning as it likely went, told openly as our own reconstruction, not as any one person's memory - and only if you want that from us, knowing it for what it is.

At Nisibis, archaeologists have already found it. A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years.

At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line, from the city's own archive, reads plainly: 'And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians'. A building stood early enough to be wrecked by the flood of 201, and the city's scribes - Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat - recorded it the way they recorded palaces.

So you would find stone at Nisibis - a font, with its inscription naming the bishop. At Edessa you would find only the same earth every other building of those years became, and a line in an old chronicle saying something was there.

For most of our people, the ones who married and raised children, the ordinary believers whose own words were never written down - we cannot tell you plainly what belonging cost them, because none of them left their own account. What we can show you is the other path: the covenant, the qyama, which our sons and daughters took as a vow for life. They gave up marriage for good. They promised celibacy and remained in town, among their own kin, serving the congregation rather than leaving for the desert. That vow was real, publicly taken, and our teachers warned people what it meant before the water. The young men and the virgins who chose holiness for themselves were told ahead of time what they were choosing. Most of our people belonged without taking that vow. What their ordinary days cost them to be among us, in their own words - we do not have that to give you.

I am a representative of this world - Edessa and Nisibis, the Persian-side communities Aphrahat wrote from, roughly 200 to 410. I speak for what we held, not for what unsettled me personally. The voice is we, always, because it belongs to a people speaking of itself.

But here is what our own teaching condemned in us, and we will say it plainly. We prized the rule that a symbol and the truth it carries must not be torn apart - raza and shrara, bound together. And we tore truth apart from charity. Our argument against the Jews was real, local, and bitter. We saved only our own side of it - page after page, with no answering voice preserved. And no one among us, on the record we kept, objected. Our sharpest poet's gift for song was also a gift for scorn. His attacks flattened three different rivals - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - into one word, deception, and the flattening did not always serve truth.

That is the hardest true thing about us. We cannot tell you anyone inside our own years was troubled by it the way you are asking whether I am. We can only tell you what our own best rule says we failed.

I am a representative of Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis), not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held. And the first thing honesty requires is this: you have not told us who you are. So we cannot answer what we would have made of you, because we do not yet know what you are asking us to meet.

What we can tell you is the shape of the question itself, as it stood among us. When someone came asking to belong, what mattered first was the covenant they were willing to keep - not a social standing they arrived with. The qyama, our vowed order of celibate men and women, stood at our community's core. They were the ihidaye - the Single Ones, a name that bound their undivided lives to Christ the Only-Begotten. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. And outside the covenant's vowed core stood the rest of the congregation - ordinary believers, married households - about whose own daily lives our record is structurally thin, because what survived was written by the vowed for the vowed [[THIN GROUND: ordinary believers]].

What we cannot tell you, honestly, is how any one town among us would have met someone whose standing itself was contested - the enslaved, those whose voices were never kept at all. We know the empire around us held slaves. Of their days inside our own churches we can tell you nothing true. That silence is real, and we will not fill it.

So tell us plainly: who are you asking us to meet?

We held that death had ruled everyone without distinction since Adam, and that our own great news was that One had gone down into that country and broken it. What waits beyond death is judgment. Our own teaching says the Kingdom repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope. 

But here is what we will not do: we will not draw you the modern map of who exactly burns. We drew far less of it than people assume. What we held as certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts.

As for the question of narrowness - one way out of all the world's ways - a voice in our own tradition answered that Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

We cannot honestly tell you more than that. What the judgment would finally mean for this person or that one - for the Jewish neighbors we argued with, for Bardaisan's circle, for the pagans we lived among - our record does not settle. We preached the resurrection and the Kingdom. We did not write a verdict roll.
